clue.text: Some show a zymurgy in extremis

definitions.text: Some show a zymurgy in extremis

parts.words: Some show a zymurgy in extremis
parts.note: reference books of words list zymurgy, the chemistry of fermentation, at their very end, as it is among the last entries from A to Z

explanation.surface: A curiosity about where an obscure brewing science turns up in a time of crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In extremis' looks like 'in dire straits', but here it means literally at the extreme end: zymurgy is one of the last words listed alphabetically.
explanation.definitionFit: Lexicons arrange words alphabetically, so a word starting ZY appears at the very end of such reference books.

clue.text: A hot time — a dumb chum can expect one

definitions.meaning: the hottest weeks of summer, linked to the rising of Sirius, the Dog Star

definitions.text: a dumb chum can expect one
definitions.meaning: a dumb chum is a pet dog, and the proverb says every dog has its day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dumb chum' is a dog, a friend that cannot speak; the proverb 'every dog has its day' promises it one day of glory.
explanation.definitionFit: The sultry midsummer period is named after Sirius the Dog Star, and the proverb gives each hound a moment of its own.

clue.text: Wayward East Loch shepherdess:

indicators.note: wayward means straying, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A shepherdess strays from a Scottish lake on its eastern shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wayward' rearranges E and LOCH. Chloe is the shepherdess in the Greek romance Daphnis and Chloe.
explanation.definitionFit: In the pastoral tale of Daphnis and Chloe, the heroine is a young woman who tends flocks.

clue.text: Gelatin contained by a tumbler it seems

parts.note: something contained by a vessel is in it
a tumbler is a drinking glass

explanation.surface: Jelly seems to be held in a drinking glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it seems' tells you to read the answer as a phrase: it IS IN GLASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Isinglass is a pure gelatine obtained from fish bladders, used to clarify beer.

clue.text: A head of cattle unwatered

definitions.meaning: an old word for an ox or cow
a drink taken undiluted is served without water

explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for bovine livestock, and spirits taken straight with no water added.

clue.text: Far from chatty when it turns up late outside

indicators.note: outside says the word for late goes around the other piece

parts.note: late in the sense of recent, as in the late developments

indicators.note: in a down clue turns up reads the little word from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Someone goes quiet when an object appears late outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses the little word 'it' (up the column in a down clue), and 'outside' wraps the word for late around that.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved person says little, so is the opposite of talkative.

clue.text: Keen-sighted upholder of Holy Writ

parts.note: a church lectern is often carved as a sharp-eyed bird of prey whose spread wings hold up the Bible

explanation.surface: A vigilant defender of the scriptures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upholder' looks like a defender of faith, but it means literally holding up: brass lecterns are often shaped as this bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird is famed for sharp vision, and church lecterns shaped like it bear the Bible on their wings.

clue.text: Battle long ago near here-still is one

definitions.text: Battle long ago near here-still is one

parts.words: Battle long ago near here-still is one
parts.note: the 1066 conflict was fought near this Sussex town, and the place where it happened is still a town named Battle nearby

explanation.surface: A tourist sign recalls an ancient fight fought close by.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1066 battle was fought a few miles away at a spot now a town called Battle, in East Sussex, a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norman Conquest battle of 1066 takes its name from this seaside town, which still lies close to the battlefield.

clue.text: Frank confession of ability and action

parts.note: to be able is can, as in I can swim
did is the past of do, the word for an action performed

explanation.surface: An honest admission: I am able, and I did it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confession of' sets the scene: the confession reads 'can and did'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone open and honest in speech is straightforward and outspoken.

clue.text: Gad about with ladies' man about tea-time

indicators.note: one word goes about, that is around, the other in this clue

parts.note: a gallant is an attentive man about town who courts women
four o'clock is tea-time, and four in Roman numerals is IV

explanation.surface: A womaniser wanders about town around the hour for afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' appears twice: the first belongs to the definition 'Gad about', the second is the container signal. British afternoon tea is traditionally taken around four o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: To gad about is to roam idly in search of pleasure, which is exactly what wandering around aimlessly means.

clue.text: A month back, the state of America's fruit

indicators.note: back says the month's abbreviation is read in reverse order

parts.note: Aug is the short form of August, a month
VA is the postal abbreviation for Virginia, a US state

explanation.surface: A reflection on an American state's produce from a month ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the month's abbreviation around, giving GUA; 'state of America' is Virginia.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropical tree's pear-shaped produce is eaten as a sweet, fragrant fruit.

clue.text: Exact retribution for, for example, Russian river reverse

indicators.note: reverse at the end says the two short pieces before it, taken together, are read backwards

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
the Neva is the river flowing through St Petersburg in Russia

explanation.surface: A demand for revenge, illustrated by a Russian river flowing the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverse' turns the run EGNEVA backwards. The first 'for' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To take revenge for a wrong is to punish the wrongdoer in return, exacting retribution on behalf of the victim.

clue.text: Performed without centre-half, it was emphasized

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the performing word goes around the other piece

parts.note: to act is to perform on stage, so performed gives acted

indicators.note: half of the word centre is taken, its first three letters

explanation.surface: A footballer's absent centre-half is blamed for a match being played with extra stress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre-half' looks like a football position, but it means half of the word centre; 'without' is the old sense of outside, so the performing word goes around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stressed syllable or word is one given prominence in speech, so stressing it means giving it emphasis.

clue.text: Where Americans are transported and Englishmen run over by vehicles

definitions.meaning: in the US this word means an underground railway system
in Britain it means a pedestrian tunnel under a road, so traffic runs over the walkers

explanation.definitionFit: Across the Atlantic it is an underground railway; in Britain the same word names a pedestrian underpass beneath traffic.

clue.text: Party with outlandish beard and pigtail

parts.note: barbe is the French word for beard, so a foreign beard
cue is an old spelling of queue, a braid of hair worn hanging down the back

explanation.surface: A party guest sports a strange beard and a plait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outlandish' looks like an anagram signal, but means foreign: French 'barbe'.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor gathering where meat is grilled over charcoal is a kind of social event.

clue.text: With list marked by pen and ruler, say

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be spoken and heard rather than spelt

parts.note: paper ruled with lines in ink is ink-lined

explanation.surface: Paper written on with a list, inked and ruled neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With list' looks like a written list, but it means leaning, as a ship lists. INK-LINED, said aloud, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship with a list leans to one side, and something leaning is tilted or sloping.

clue.text: Kind of binding — by Eve's needle and thread ?

definitions.text: Kind of binding — by Eve's needle and thread

parts.words: Kind of binding — by Eve's needle and thread
parts.note: a type of book binding with removable pages, and Eve stitching fig leaves together loosely in Genesis

explanation.surface: A bookbinder's method credited to the first woman's sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together; her rough stitching would leave a leaf loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A folder with detachable sheets has this style of binding, and Eve's fig-leaf garment would have been sewn loosely.

clue.text: Time-honoured Lancaster permitted the challenge

parts.note: Shakespeare's Richard II opens with 'Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd Lancaster'
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: An aged duke allowed a challenge to proceed.
explanation.walkthrough: John of Gaunt was Duke of Lancaster; Shakespeare calls him 'time-honour'd Lancaster'.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing down an armoured glove was the medieval way to issue a challenge to combat.

clue.text: Capital fellow is shown in a type of marble

indicators.note: shown in says one word is displayed within the other

parts.note: Parian marble is the fine white stone quarried on the Greek island of Paros

explanation.surface: A fine fellow is put on display in a marble statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital fellow' sounds like praise for a splendid chap, but it means a man from a capital, Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the French capital is called by this name, so he is a man of a capital city.

clue.text: Every year a god enters the temple

indicators.note: enters says the deity goes inside the other piece

parts.note: p.a. abbreviates per annum, Latin for each year

explanation.surface: Once a year a deity visits the shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enters' puts A GOD inside PA.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiered tower found in East Asia, used as a Buddhist shrine, is a kind of temple.

clue.text: Hardy heroin: has work, but turned to drink

indicators.note: turned says the combined letters are read back to front

parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles is the heroine of Thomas Hardy's novel; the page prints heroin for heroine
op. abbreviates opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A tough drug addict takes a job but turns to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses TESS + OP. The page prints 'heroin' where the wordplay needs 'heroine', giving a drug-themed surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A posset is an old hot beverage of milk curdled with ale or wine.

clue.text: The approaching dark

parts.note: the coming hours of darkness, this evening still to come

explanation.surface: A phrase for night drawing in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dark' stands for night, so the approaching dark is the coming night, this evening.
explanation.definitionFit: This evening's darkness is still ahead, coming nearer as the day ends.

clue.text: Hello ! In tears, lassie ?

definitions.meaning: a word of welcome is a salutation
in Scots, to greet is to weep, so a crying Scottish girl is said to be ...

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lassie' signals Scots, where 'greet' means to cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying hello is a salutation; and in Scottish dialect, weeping is described with the same word.

clue.text: The thank-you letter

parts.note: ta is informal British for thank you

explanation.surface: A note sent to say thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The thank-you letter' looks like a note of gratitude, but 'letter' is a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Lower churchman takes me in

indicators.note: takes, completed by in, says the churchman admits the other word inside
in completes takes in, a phrase for enclosing something

parts.note: a dean is a senior clergyman in charge of a cathedral

explanation.surface: A clergyman is fooled into lowering himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes me in' looks like 'deceives me', but it is a container signal: the churchman encloses the word me.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower oneself in dignity is to degrade or debase oneself.

clue.text: Miss Heath, age about one hundred

indicators.note: about says the period of time goes around the other letters

parts.note: an era is an age or period of history
I is the Roman numeral one
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A woman named Heath is described as almost a century old.
explanation.walkthrough: Erica is both a girl's name, Miss, and the botanical genus of heath plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name that is also the Latin genus of heathers, so a lady called heather.

clue.text: "A tall ship and a —— to steer her by" (Masefield)

definitions.text: A tall ship and a —— to steer her by

parts.words: A tall ship and a —— to steer her by
parts.note: a line from John Masefield's poem Sea-Fever with the word for a sailor's guiding light in the sky left out

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from a famous poem about longing for the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masefield's Sea-Fever reads 'And all I ask is a tall ship and a star to steer her by'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors navigated by celestial bodies, so a bright one in the night sky guides the ship.

clue.text: The devil of a card !

definitions.meaning: ... is an old euphemism for the devil, as in what the ...
a playing card with two pips is called a two or a ...

explanation.definitionFit: The word is a mild oath standing in for the Devil, and also the name for the two in a pack of playing cards.

clue.text: Characterization of a ' sign-writer ?

parts.note: characterization read as the forming of characters, the letters a painter of shop signs draws

explanation.surface: A question about how a signpainter would be portrayed in fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characterization' suggests portraying a person, but here it is making characters, that is letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A signpainter's craft is forming characters, so the letters drawn are the product of the trade.

clue.text: What actually, happened : is prosaic

definitions.meaning: prosaic means plain, unimaginative and practical

explanation.definitionFit: A real event is a factual matter, and an unemotional, practical manner is described with the same hyphenated phrase.
